content: The burden of tuberculosis (TB) and the role of community supervisors in directly observed therapy (DOT) strategies have been extensively studied. Research has evaluated the efficacy of community-based versus institutional-based DOT for short-course TB treatment in various settings, such as the Kilombero district in Tanzania. Randomized controlled trials have also compared the effectiveness of community health workers versus family members in supervising TB treatment, as seen in studies conducted in Nepal and other regions. Community-based approaches have shown significant improvements in TB case notification and treatment outcomes, particularly in resource-limited settings like Southern Ethiopia. Innovative interventions, such as food incentives, financial support, and mobile phone reminders, have been implemented to enhance adherence to TB treatment, especially among vulnerable populations, including homeless patients in Russia and migrant workers in Shanghai. Studies have also explored the integration of TB treatment into community-based home care programs for individuals living with HIV/AIDS, as demonstrated in Zambia. The cost-effectiveness of home-based care compared to hospital care for chronically ill TB patients has been analyzed in Botswana, highlighting the potential for reducing healthcare costs while maintaining treatment success. The use of technology, such as video directly observed therapy (VDOT) and electronic reminders, has been piloted in urban settings like New York City to improve medication adherence. Similarly, text messaging interventions and automated telephone reminders have been tested to support TB treatment adherence in various populations. The role of lay health workers and community volunteers in supporting TB treatment adherence has been studied in South Africa and Thailand, demonstrating the importance of community engagement in TB control efforts. Financial incentives and transportation subsidies have also been shown to improve treatment outcomes among internal migrants in urban areas. In addition to community-based interventions, the effectiveness of fixed-dose combination (FDC) formulations versus separate drug formulations for TB treatment has been evaluated. Studies have also investigated the impact of intermittent dosing during the intensive phase of treatment compared to daily dosing for drug-susceptible pulmonary TB. Guidelines for the treatment of drug-susceptible and multidrug-resistant TB have been updated, incorporating evidence from systematic reviews and meta-analyses. The use of newer drugs, such as bedaquiline and delamanid, has been recommended for the treatment of multidrug-resistant TB, based on interim policy guidance. The involvement of community members, health workers, and innovative technologies in TB care has been critical in addressing challenges related to treatment adherence, default rates, and healthcare access. This transformation provides a clear and professional summary of the key points from the references and guidelines, focusing on the specific interventions and findings related to TB treatment and care.
